history.content: What could happen to Detroit Municipal bonds because of Detroit's filing for bankruptcy?

If the courts process Detroit's bankruptcy as expected, there could be a couple of scenarios for the Detroit Municipal bonds. Firstly, if the city is allowed to discharge its short-term and long-term debt, the bonds could become worthless. Secondly, even if the city can only restructure the debt, bondholders will likely have to accept large concessions. However, the market for these bonds may be limited, and the potential loss may not be immediately reflected in bond prices. The market's perception of the risk associated with these bonds could change based on factors such as federal or state aid, which may impact the bond prices.

evidence.text: There are a few different ways to organize this, but mostly I think you need to talk to a lawyer.  The 50/50 split thing should be in writing along with a bunch of other issues. You could have one of you doing a sole proprietorship where the other person is a contractor that receives half of all revenues/profits.  The person that owns the sole proprietorship may be entitled to deduct certain costs of running the entity.  The other person would then be 1099'd his share of revenues. You could set up a partnership, again legal paperwork is necessary. You could also setup an S-Corp, where each of you is a 50% owner. You could also setup an LLC that is organized as any of the above.  I would only do this if you can self fund some additional tax preparation costs.  Figure about $600/year at a minimum.   There are a lot of options with a sole proprietorship being the easiest.  Your first step on the new venture would be to apply for an EIN (free), and then opening a business bank account.

If you trust the other party, an international bank wire would be the quickest, easiest, and cheapest option. It is the standard way to pay for something overseas from the United States. Unfortunately, in most cases, they are not reversible. I don't believe Paypal is an option for an amount that large.  Escrow companies do exist, but you would have to research those on a case by case basis to see if any fit the criteria for your transaction and the countries involved. I'll also add:  If it were me, and there was no way to get references or verify the person's identity and intent to my satisfaction, then I would probably consider hopping on a plane. For that amount of money, I would verify the person and items are legitimate, in person, and then wire the money.

I'm not sure there is good data on Kiva, etc, but P2P microlending site Prosper has released their data. The default rates are evidently fairly high. For borrowers in the 'developed' world (the target audience of Prosper), other sources of credit are available (e.g. banks); one has to suspect, then, that borrowers on Prosper are considered too risky for bank loans.
